blocks.prompt: The Tower That Talks to Ships
blocks.text: A lighthouse is a tall tower by the sea. Near the shore there are rocks hiding under the water. A boat can hit them in the dark. So we build a lighthouse and put a bright light at the top. The light turns in a slow circle. From a boat far away, it looks like the light is blinking. Sailors watch for it. They know that flash means keep away from here. Long ago, a keeper lived inside the tower. Every night the keeper climbed the stairs and lit the lamp. Now most lighthouses turn themselves on.

blocks.prompt: How a Lighthouse Says Its Own Name
blocks.text: At night, one light on a dark coast looks much like another. That was a real problem for sailors. A captain could see a light and still not know which light it was, or which rocks it was warning about. So lighthouse builders gave every tower its own pattern of flashes. One might flash once every ten seconds. Another might send two quick flashes, then wait. A sailor pulled out a watch, counted the seconds, and looked the pattern up in a book called a light list. The pattern told him exactly where he was. Daytime needed a different trick. In daylight the beam is useless, so the tower itself has to be the signal. That is why lighthouses wear such strange paint. One is candy striped in red and white. One is checkered. Cape Hatteras in North Carolina is wrapped in a black and white spiral. Those patterns are called daymarks, and along one stretch of coast, no two are the same. A lighthouse is really one message sent two ways: you are here, and the rocks are close.

answers: every light looked the same, so he could not tell which rocks it warned about
he timed the flashes with a watch and looked the pattern up in a light list
the painted pattern on the tower; it is needed in daylight when the beam is useless

notes: A Fresnel lens is rings of prisms

Keepers were nicknamed wickies
The light never blinks, the beam sweeps

blocks.prompt: The Lens That Bends the Light
blocks.text: A flame does not aim. Put a lamp at the top of a tower and its light spills out in every direction, up into the clouds, down onto the rocks, out to sea. Only a sliver of it ever reaches a ship. For hundreds of years that was the best anyone could do. Keepers burned wood, then coal, then whale oil, and captains squinted for a smudge of orange on the horizon. In 1822 a French engineer named Augustin Fresnel solved it. He built a lens out of rings. Each ring is a prism, a wedge of glass that bends light as it passes through, and every ring is angled a little differently. Light that would have escaped upward gets bent down. Light heading for the floor gets bent up. All of it leaves the lens together in one flat, hard beam. A Fresnel lens can be twelve feet tall and still weigh far less than a solid lens of the same power would. It turned a candle into a searchlight. Then came the second problem: the beam had to sweep. So engineers borrowed from clocks. A heavy weight hung on a chain down the middle of the tower. As the weight sank, it turned gears, and the gears turned the whole lens around the lamp. The keeper wound that weight back up every few hours, all night, every night. He also trimmed the lamp wick, which is why keepers were nicknamed wickies. The light never blinked. It swung, like a slow arm, past you and away.

blocks.prompt: Building on a Rock That Disappears
blocks.text: Eleven miles off the east coast of Scotland there is a reef called the Bell Rock. For most of the day it does not exist. At high tide the sea closes over it completely, and a ship can sail across the spot without seeing a thing. Then the tide falls, the rock surfaces, and any ship that misjudged the water is opened up like a tin can. For centuries it was the most feared hazard on that coast. The obvious answer was a lighthouse. The obvious objection was that you cannot build on a foundation that is underwater most of the time. Robert Stevenson took the job anyway. Work began in 1807. His crews could only cut stone on the rock during the few hours around low tide, and when the water came back they rowed to a ship anchored nearby and waited. Later they built a wooden hut on stilts above the reef so they could sleep over the waves instead of losing hours to the crossing. Every block of granite was shaped on shore first, then floated out and locked into its neighbors with dovetail joints, the same interlocking pattern a carpenter uses, cut into stone. Nothing held the tower together but its own weight and the shape of the blocks. The mortar was hydraulic lime, a cement that hardens underwater rather than dissolving. The light first shone in 1811. It is still shining. The Bell Rock Lighthouse is the oldest sea washed lighthouse left standing anywhere, and in more than two hundred years of storms the tower has never needed its stonework rebuilt. What Stevenson understood was that the sea does not push a tower over. It pulls it apart, block by block, finding the weak seam. So he built a tower with no weak seams. Everything since, every rock lighthouse on every dangerous reef, is a variation on that idea. The keepers are gone now, replaced by machines and solar panels, but the stone they were sent to live in is exactly where they left it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Cape Hatteras Light: 198 feet of brick
About 1.25 million bricks
Moved 2,900 feet inland in 1999
The move took 23 days
Diamond Shoals reach 14 miles out to sea
Boston Light is the last staffed US lighthouse

blocks.prompt: The Lighthouse That Walked Inland
blocks.text: Every lighthouse is an argument with the ocean, and the ocean is patient. Cape Hatteras sits on a thin curve of sand off North Carolina, and just offshore, hidden under the swell, lie the Diamond Shoals: shifting sandbars that reach almost fourteen miles out to sea. Two ocean currents collide there, the warm Gulf Stream running north and the cold Labrador Current running south, and the sand they carry piles into ridges that move. Hundreds of ships have been lost on them. Sailors named that stretch of coast the Graveyard of the Atlantic, and they were not being dramatic. The lighthouse built to answer the Shoals was lit in 1870. At 198 feet it is the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States, roughly 1.25 million bricks wrapped in a black and white spiral so that captains could identify it in daylight, when its beam is worthless. At the top sat a first order Fresnel lens: a barrel of glass rings, each one a prism angled to catch light that would otherwise have wandered off into the sky and bend it flat, out toward the horizon. The lens did not blink. It rotated, and what a sailor twenty miles offshore saw as a flash was simply the beam sweeping past his eye. It worked. What nobody had solved was the ground. Barrier islands are not land in the way a continent is land. They are sand in transit, pushed and rebuilt by every storm, and the Atlantic side of Hatteras had been eating itself westward for as long as anyone had measured it. When the tower was built it stood about 1,500 feet from the water. By the 1930s the sea was at its base. Engineers fought back for sixty years with groins, sandbags, and artificial dunes, and the ocean took all of it. By the 1980s the argument was over. The shoreline had closed to about 120 feet. One serious hurricane would have finished the job. So in 1999 they moved it. The tower weighs roughly 4,800 tons and is made of brick, a material with no interest in being flexible. Movers cut it free of its foundation, slid steel beams beneath it, lifted the whole thing on hydraulic jacks, and pushed it along a track of steel rails in five foot increments, leapfrogging the rails forward as it went. It traveled 2,900 feet inland over twenty three days. The crack that everyone dreaded never appeared. The light was relit on its new foundation, a little over half a mile from where it had stood for 129 years, and the beach it left behind is now underwater. There is an obvious question hiding in all that effort. Ships do not need Cape Hatteras any more. A modern vessel knows where it is to within a few feet from satellites, in fog, at night, in weather that would have hidden any beam ever built. The Fresnel lens is a museum piece. Most lighthouses were automated decades ago and their keepers sent home, and the last staffed light in the United States is Boston Light, which is staffed because Congress passed a law saying so, not because anyone needs a person there. Which means the move was not really about navigation. We spent millions of dollars and twenty three days walking a brick tower across a sand dune to preserve a machine we had already replaced. That is worth sitting with. A lighthouse is one of the few structures humans build purely for the benefit of strangers they will never meet, and switching it off, or letting the sea have it, would say something we were not ready to say. The Shoals are still there. The current still runs. And the argument with the ocean, which the ocean is winning, has simply been carried a little further up the beach.
